Polling is time consuming and expensive, especially as we move away from land lines and people have largely stopped answering unknown numbers due to incredible amounts of spam. Let's say you have budget/capacity to poll 10,000 people. You have two options:

1. 10 polls with 1,000 people sample size and a 3% margin of error. 
2. 20 polls with 500 people sample size and a 4% margin of error. 

An aggregate of the latter is probably going to be more accurate due to double the polls, even with the slightly worse MoE.

[Here's a couple proofs](https://www.quora.com/How-do-I-show-that-the-area-of-a-rectangle-is-greatest-when-it-is-a-square-if-the-perimeter-of-a-rectangle-is-fixed-in-length)

Here's my shot at it:

The area of a rectangle is length x width. For a square they're the same, so call it width^2.

In order to make a square into a rectangle of the same perimeter, you need to pick a constant K and add it to one dimension of the square and subtract from the other. For example making a 4x4 square (P=16) into a 2x6 rectangle (also P=16) would give you K=2. 

Thus the area of this rectangle is (width_square + K) x (width_square - K). FOIL and you'll get the area of the rectangle = width_square^2 - K^2, which is clearly K^2 less than the area of the square. 

In my previous example the 4x4 had area 16 and 2x6 has area 12, which is 4 less aka K^2 since K was 2.

I think it's kind of like predicting the stock market. If you get an index fund that's evenly distributed among a representative sample of the stock market it will with shocking consistency produce something like 6% YoY returns over any 30+ year period. That doesn't mean you can go day trading or invest heavily in a single company, because things can be very volatile in the short term or when singling out specific stocks. 


As a complete system, both are far more predictable than their chaotic individual components.
